About me

I'm a Level 7 qualified Business Analyst with over four years of experience spanning enterprise technology, consulting and operations.

All case studies
Blue Lagoon Fish and Chips, Glasgow

Solving a cold food complaint pattern

Customers kept complaining about cold food. I used delivery data to find out why.

SPSSCluster analysisProcess redesign

The problem

Customers kept reporting that delivery orders arrived cold, and the complaints were clustered rather than random.

What I did

Ran cluster analysis in SPSS on delivery postcodes to group them into regions, then matched complaints against those regions.

What changed

Nearby postcode orders now go out together on shared runs, and outlying areas get extra time built in. The recurring complaint pattern was resolved.

See the fix in action

Every house is a delivery order from the Blue Lagoon shop, labelled by postcode area around East Kilbride. Switch between how deliveries worked before and after the change.

0trips out of the shop
0orders at risk of arriving cold
Arrives hot At risk of arriving cold Extra time planned

Blackmont Consulting, client Bridgify (formerly Flats4You)

Taking a student housing and jobs platform to the UK market

A startup had an idea: one place where international students find a home and part time work. I helped turn it into a launch plan backed by evidence.

Primary researchSWOTCompetitor benchmarkingUK complianceGo to market

The problem

Bridgify needed to know what international students actually struggle with, who it was up against, and what it would take to launch legally and credibly in the UK.

What I did

Ran a primary survey of international students, benchmarked twelve student housing brands on digital performance, built a SWOT, and mapped UK GDPR, employment law and student visa work limits into a compliance checklist.

What changed

A full market entry strategy: a pilot launch in Aberdeen, an advertising plan matched to budget and timeline, five routes to job partnerships, and data security and UX recommendations.

MSc research project, Stirling Council area

Health insight for smaller Scottish towns

Health outcomes in Stirling change from one town to the next. I used geodemographic and hospital data to show where the pressure sits and what policymakers could do about it.

CRISP-DMPower BIACORN geodemographicsData cleaningComparative analysis

The problem

Stirling mixes remote rural communities with dense, deprived urban estates. The research asked how socio-economic and environmental conditions combine to shape health, and what interventions would narrow the gap.

What I did

Followed the CRISP-DM process. I cleaned and joined CACI’s ACORN geodemographic data with census and hospital data on alcohol related conditions, then built Power BI dashboards comparing wards, school catchments, community councils and three hospitals.

What changed

Targeted recommendations for two very different places: better transport, mobile care and telehealth for rural Aberfoyle and Strathfillan, and integrated care, mental health support and healthier retail zoning for Raploch and Cornton.

MSc client project, ACS Clothing

Closing the gender gap at a B Corp

A sustainable fashion company had signed every pledge on gender equality. The data showed where the pledges weren't reaching.

Stakeholder interviewsGap analysisPower interest gridSODALDA topic modelling

The problem

ACS Clothing wanted to improve its B Corp gender equality score and align with SDG 5, but women held only 10% of leadership roles and some departments were almost entirely one gender.

What I did

Interviewed 11 staff across five departments plus the COO, logged 17 gaps with owners and actions, mapped stakeholders by power and interest, built SODA cognitive maps, and ran LDA topic modelling on the transcripts.

What changed

A client report for the COO with four priorities: internal leadership pipelines with mentoring, inclusive culture training, a women led sustainability task force, and continuous monitoring through scenario planning.

MSc group consulting project, Haggis Hoppers taxis

Putting taxis where the demand is

A Glasgow taxi firm had a month of call data and one question: how many cars, where, and when?

Time seriesForecastingGeospatial analysisK-means clusteringBalanced scorecard

The problem

Haggis Hoppers was allocating drivers without a clear view of when calls peaked or where pickups clustered, leaving customers waiting at busy times and cars idle at quiet ones.

What we did

As a team of seven, we analysed February call data by hour and day, built a next day hourly forecast, mapped pickups and drop offs as a heatmap, clustered them into five zones, and linked it all in a balanced scorecard.

What changed

We recommended dynamic fleet allocation: forecast the drivers needed each hour and reset cars to the centre of their zone after every trip, backed by a lean approach to cut waste and a reward scheme for drivers.

February, one call at a time

Daily calls against the monthly average. Hover or tap a day. The spikes weren't random, and that's what made demand forecastable.

Tap a day to see its calls.

MSc consulting proposal, Frazer-Nash Consultancy brief

Scoping a pathway to nuclear energy in Scotland

A politically sensitive question, a public that has long said no, and a client asking how management science could help. My answer was a costed, phased plan.

Scenario planningPESTLEStakeholder gridCost benefit analysisSensitivity analysisProject planning

The brief

Frazer-Nash invited proposals on how Scotland could build nuclear capability, given long standing government and public resistance on safety, waste and cost.

What I did

Wrote an individual proposal targeting two of the brief's questions: the long term strategic role of nuclear, and its economic and environmental impact. I designed the method, schedule and effort estimate for each phase.

The proposal

An 11 month, two phase engagement. Phase one: scenario planning and stakeholder engagement strategy. Phase two: cost benefit analysis stress tested with sensitivity analysis. Three reports and two presentations.

The plan, month by month

Every month had defined activities and estimated hours. Tap a month to open it.

How the scenarios get built
  1. Find driving forces with PESTLE
  2. Cluster related forces
  3. Plot on an impact and uncertainty matrix
  4. Take the two most impactful, most uncertain
  5. Cross their outcomes into four futures
MSc group case study set by Deloitte, regional police force

Finding the missing 98 officers

A police force knew it was short staffed. The HR data said by how much, once we fixed the errors in it.

Data validationETLFTE gap analysisThematic analysisTalent managementADDIE

The problem

Three regional forces faced high vacancies, resignations and a growing digital crime threat. Leadership needed the staffing gap quantified by region and role before deciding where to act.

What we did

As a team of eight, we rebuilt the HR delta calculations from scratch, found and corrected errors in the client's own totals, and analysed planned against actual FTE for every role. Interview transcripts went through thematic analysis to explain the numbers.

What changed

A three phase roadmap: retain and upskill current officers, redesign hiring for new recruits, and build a dedicated digital crime capability using the ADDIE training model.

Where the gaps really are

Planned posts against actual staff, role by role. Pick a region.

558planned FTE
460actual FTE
18%understaffed

The roadmap

  1. Retain

    Recognition tied to cases solved and response times, bonus and retirement plans, and continuous digital skills training. Built on Maslow's hierarchy of needs.

  2. Recruit

    Redesigned sergeant KPIs, hackathons and internships to attract tech talent, and training that runs alongside onboarding. Built on the talent management model.

  3. Reinforce

    A central digital crime unit with private sector expertise and a real time helpline for officers. Designed with the ADDIE model.

Internship, Amadeus Software Labs, 2020

Clearing technical debt from 16,000 files

A legacy codebase too big to clean by hand. I built a tool to do it, and found a governance gap along the way.

PythonC++ guidelinesAutomationClang formatPull requestsTraceability matrix

The problem

A monolithic commercial codebase of over 16,000 files still carried old C style patterns. Developers were moving to modern C++ guidelines, but fixing ten categories of debt by hand was impossible at that volume.

What I did

Ran a feasibility study on each debt category, then built a Python tool that takes a file owner and a category, rewrites the code, formats and builds it, and raises a pull request for the owner to review.

What changed

4,729 files and 60,258 lines modernised through 171 pull requests. I also found 230 files with no owner, whose changes were merging unreviewed, and fixed ownership through six pull requests.
